{{Short description|Southern African chemist, Cricket official, and diplomat}}

{{Use South African English|date=October 2023}}
'''Krish Mackerdhuj''' (15 August 1939 – 26 May 2004) was a South African chemist, [[cricket]] official, and diplomat.

==Early life==
Mackerdhuj was born on 15 August 1939 in [[Durban]], [[Natal Province]].<ref name=cricinfo>{{cite news|url=https://www.espncricinfo.com/player/krish-mackerdhuj-294505|title=Krish Mackerdhuj|publisher=ESPNcricinfo|accessdate=19 October 2022}}</ref> He attended Sastri College in Durban and later completed the degree of Bachelor of Science at [[Fort Hare University]]. He worked as a chemical technologist for Shell and BP.<ref name=iol>{{cite news|url=https://www.iol.co.za/capeargus/sport/former-ucb-president-krish-mackerdhuj-dies-535328|title=Former UCB president Krish Mackerdhuj dies|publisher=IOL|date=26 May 2004|accessdate=19 October 2022|first=Patrick|last=Compton}}</ref>

==Cricket==
Mackerdhuj played club cricket in Durban but retired due to injury.<ref name=iol/> He umpired nine matches of [[first-class cricket]].<ref name=cricinfo/> In the 1970s and 1980s he was a member of the South African Council on Sport (SACOS), which was recognised as the sporting arm of the anti-apartheid movement.<ref name=iol/> He was president of the multiracial South African Cricket Board (SACB) from 1984 to 1991.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/cricket/3751199.stm|title=SA pioneer Mackerdhuj dies|date=26 May 2004|accessdate=19 October 2022|publisher=BBC News}}</ref> In the lead-up to the end of [[apartheid]], Mackerdhuj played a key role in the merger of SACB and the predominantly white South African Cricket Union (SACU). Mackerdhuj was subsequently elected as the first president of the [[United Cricket Board of South Africa]] in 1992. Along with [[Ali Bacher]], he successfully lobbied for South Africa to be awarded the hosting rights for the [[2003 Cricket World Cup]].<ref name=vice>{{cite news|url=https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/the-smiling-face-of-south-african-cricket-141226|title=The smiling face of South African cricket|first=Telford|last=Vice|publisher=ESPNcricinfo|date=26 May 2004|accessdate=19 October 2022}}</ref>

==Other activities==
Mackerdhuj served as South Africa's ambassador to Japan from 1998 to 2003.<ref name=vice/> He was later asked to serve as ambassador to Uzbekistan, but declined the position due to illness.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraphindia.com/sports/mackerdhuj-passes-away/cid/1046267|title=Mackerdhuj passes away|newspaper=The Telegraph|location=Kolkata|date=27 May 2004|accessdate=19 October 2022}}</ref>

==Personal life and legacy==
Mackerdhuj died on 26 May 2004 at St Augustine's Hospital, Durban. He had suffered a mild heart attack two months earlier. He was survived by his wife Sminthra and sons Prashim and Avin.<ref name=iol/>

In January 2011, South Africa hosted India for a [[Indian cricket team in South Africa in 2010–11#Only T20I|one-off Twenty20 International]] in Durban, the winner of which was awarded the Krish Mackerdhuj Trophy.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.espncricinfo.com/story/south-africa-set-to-host-india-in-one-off-t20-in-january-460479|title=South Africa set to host India in one-off T20 in January|publisher=ESPNcricinfo|date=21 May 2010|accessdate=19 October 2022}}</ref>
